pr_title: Enable dynamic configuration of service account names and audiences for token requests in node audience restriction
pr_body:
Allow for dynamically configuring service accounts and audiences for which kubelet can request a token for as part of the node audience restriction feature.

1. Allow any audience for any service account
```yaml
rules:
- verbs: ["request-serviceaccounts-token-audience"]
  apiGroups: [""]
  # wildcard for audiences
  resources: ["*"]
  # unrestricted resourceNames allows all service account names
```

2. Allow any audience for a specific service account `mysa`
```yaml
rules:
- verbs: ["request-serviceaccounts-token-audience"]
  apiGroups: [""]
  # wildcard for audiences
  resources: ["*"]
  resourceNames: ["mysa"]
```

3. Allow a specific audience `myaudience` for any service account
```yaml
rules:
- verbs: ["request-serviceaccounts-token-audience"]
  apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["myaudience"]
  # unrestricted resourceNames allows all service account names
```

4. Allow a specific audience `myaudience` for a specific service account `mysa`
```yaml
rules:
- verbs: ["request-serviceaccounts-token-audience"]
  apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["myaudience"]
  resourceNames: ["mysa"]
```

5. Allow API server audience for all service accounts
```yaml
rules:
- verbs: ["request-serviceaccounts-token-audience"]
  apiGroups: [""]
  resources: [""]
  # unrestricted resourceNames allows all service account names
```


fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/128678

/kind feature
/sig auth
/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

```release-note
Allow for dynamic configuration of service account name and audience kubelet can request a token for as part of the node audience restriction feature.
```

```docs
[KEP]: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-auth/4412-projected-service-account-tokens-for-kubelet-image-credential-providers/README.md
```

I think the approach of a synthetic authz check is reasonable.

My goals for the particular mapping we choose are to be as closely connected to the real request attributes as we can and have a plausible rationale for the mapping we chose where we differ.

I think we can use the real request's API group, service account name, and service account namespace, and get all the use cases satisfied with only changing the verb and resource.

Making the audience the resource seems like the only reasonable way to get the wildcard and specific matching we need out of RBAC, so let's continue with that approach.

That leaves the verb to describe what the heck the resource is _and_ what you're doing with it.

The way I would describe this in english is: "requesting a service account token audience"

The real REST resource they're hitting is "serviceaccounts/token", so maybe we can transform that into the verb to give *some* connection to the real REST resource.

I would suggest this in the subject access review:
```
Verb: request-serviceaccounts-token-audience
Resource: $audience
APIGroup: $request.apiGroup (which is the service account API group)
Name: $request.name (which is the service account name)
Namespace: $request.namespace (which is the service account namespace)
```

issue_context.title: [KEP-4412] Enable dynamic configuration of service account names and audiences for token requests in node audience restriction
issue_context.body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128077 has been merged, and starting in v1.32, we are enforcing restrictions on the audiences for which the kubelet can request tokens.

Add new KAS flag that allows configuring list of permitted audiences specifically for image pulls.

/sig auth
/kind feature
/assign
comments: For visibility, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128077 broke one of our node daemons using kubelet credentials to provision workload identity tokens for a workload identity audience. Before the escape hatch graduates / locks on, we either need a reasonable path to giving scoped service account token creation access to a daemonset (something along the lines of https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4935) or a way to indicate audiences that should be allowed in addition to the API-visible ones (maybe a more general form of what this issue is tracking).

I think a kube-apiserver flag would be sufficient for our purposes in GKE, but in general, users may run arbitrary daemonsets that reuse kubelet credentials to take advantage of node restriction.  These daemonsets might be minting tokens to talk to other external services (and thus need to set their own audiences).

So we probably need either:

* A mechanism accessible to the "cluster administrator" persona (as distinct from the "platform provider" persona) to set a list of allowed audiences for node identities to request, or
* Some sort of first-class node-restricted daemonset feature so that they no longer have to steal Kubelet's identity.

> * Some sort of first-class node-restricted daemonset feature so that they no longer have to steal Kubelet's identity.

https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4935 is aiming to provide this, but would likely lean on running those restricted service accounts through NodeRestriction admission, so *that* would need some way to know about acceptable audiences in addition to API-visible ones

> * A mechanism accessible to the "cluster administrator" persona (as distinct from the "platform provider" persona) to set a list of allowed audiences for node identities to request

Yeah, I think we need something around this
Would it make sense to add something on the ServiceAccount resource for specifying additional allowed audiences (beyond pod volumes)?
(I think we still need the kube-apiserver flag, but maybe ServiceAccount can be the place for custom audience config)

> broke one of our node daemons using kubelet credentials to provision workload identity tokens for a workload identity audience

Could the associated pod be updated to include a projected SA token volume with the desired audience?

That might work in common cases, but I think there may be some edge cases with our daemon where the audiences are dynamic, depending on annotations on other resources or some other config, where we wouldn't want to redeploy the daemon just to allow a new audience. @ahmedtd (I admit, restarting kube-apiserver isn't great either).

An extension of ServiceAccount might work for these cases as well...

@mtaufen @ahmedtd regarding the case where you have a daemon using node creds to provision SA tokens, is it safe to assume that the daemon is getting those SA tokens for it own SA (i.e. only the audience is dynamic and not the SA itself)?  If so, couldn't you simply:

1. Create a role / role binding to grant that daemon's SA the ability to create tokens for itself (these would have no audience restriction because the caller isn't a node)
2. Let the kubelet provision the daemon's SA token as normal
3. Use the daemon's SA token to create more tokens for the daemon SA with any audience you need

I suspect this would be a minor change to the daemon's code (it would have two REST clients instead of one) but it would work on any version of Kube.

No, the SA is dynamic.  The daemon in question is serving a local RPC interface that other pods on the node use to retrieve their *own* credentials.

So if a pod running as service account `foo/bar` makes a request to the daemon, then the daemon requests a token for `foo/bar` with a specific, fixed audience.

(The token is then exchange for a Google access token representing the pod's identity in GCP IAM).

Edit: Flow diagram: https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity#credential-flow

Okay, thanks for the info, I understand the flow now.  @aramase and I have worked out a lightweight approach to allow for both dynamic service accounts and dynamic audiences.  Will open PRs after the holiday season.
We have a PR open for this now: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130485.

review_comments: Please add a test for the API server audience via `""`.

In addition to what you have below, have the test assert that exact `authorizer.Attributes` it saw.  That guarantees we cover every field (for example the user info isn't being asserted right now) and guarantees that the unit tests will fail if any part of the SAR is accidentally changed (since that would break our API).
This is currently testing allowing `audience1` with any service account called `default` in all namespaces.  I think that is structurally valid, just not sure who would use the feature this way.
I would expect each of these tests to start with the inverse of the check to prove that creating the RBAC is what actually caused the test to pass.
